title: Evening (II.11)
hookLine: the replay of a bad day starts at lights-out; Francis de Sales puts thanks in front of it
tomorrow: no time to pray between class, lifts and practice. or is there?

cards: Lights off, and the replay starts. The thing you said at lunch. The look on someone's face.
The message you shouldn't have sent. On a bad day, the mind goes straight to the wreckage. Francis de Sales puts something odd in front of it.
His evening exercise, the other bookend to the morning, begins with thanks. Not after the look back. Before it.
Even on the days that went badly. Why that order?

teach.b: Start a little earlier than bedtime. Francis suggests a short pause before supper, a few minutes back in God's company, so the day's prayer doesn't stop at breakfast. Then, before sleep, the order he gives.
Thanks first: thank God for keeping you through the day.
Only then the look back, and he makes it easy: think where you were, who you were with, what you did. Catholics call this the examination of conscience. Whatever good you find, thank God for it.
Whatever went wrong, ask his pardon, resolve to confess it when you can, and set it right with care.

Then the last step: commend to God's Providence your body and soul, the Church, your family and your friends. Ask Our Lady, your guardian angel and the saints to watch over you, and go to rest with God's blessing.

So here's one way to read the puzzle. Thanks first means you never walk into the review empty-handed; the wrong things get looked at from inside a day that also held gifts. And the night doesn't end on the replay.
It ends on handing over. The morning offered a day not yet lived. The evening gives back the one that was, good and bad together.

how: Some Catholics make a short examination of conscience before sleep, giving thanks, looking back over the day and asking pardon; some families say night prayers together.

o: a short night exercise: thanks, a look back, rest
the hour of prayer said at sunset in a monastery
a vigil Mass on the night before a feast day

games.q: the evening, step by step — tap the pairs.
p: a short pause in God's company
where, with whom, what you did
commend everyone to Providence, then rest

s: for Francis, the examination of conscience is only a list of sins
it starts with thanks, and good things found get thanked for too.
he suggests a short pause before supper as well as prayer at bedtime
so the day's prayer doesn't stop at breakfast.
the evening exercise ends with the review of faults
it ends with everything commended to God's Providence, and rest with his blessing.

games.q: your friend keeps a nightly journal that is only a list of what she did wrong. she feels worse every night. what would Francis's evening change first?
o: start each entry with what she's grateful for.
stop journaling; looking back is the problem.
add more detail to every mistake so she learns.
games.why: Francis keeps the look back but puts thanks in front of it, and ends with handing the day over, not with the list.

practice: Count three good things from today on your fingers; small ones count. Then walk back once through where you were and with whom, and name one thing to set right. If you pray, you can hand the people you love to God by name.

wordCard.voice: Evening. In the Introduction, the day's last exercise: thanks, a look back, pardon asked, and everything handed over before sleep.

orig.note: Latin: examination of conscience, the prayerful look back over the day.

carryVoice: Keep this one: hand him the day, the good and the bad in the same two hands. Sleep well.
